sources.title: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)
sources.status: In force. Most provisions commenced on 1 July 2020, with a 12-month transition period that ended on 30 June 2021. Enforced by the Information Regulator.

sources.title: Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000 (PAIA)
sources.status: In force. Gives a right of access to records held by public and private bodies, subject to grounds for refusal. The Information Regulator oversees PAIA compliance, including PAIA manuals.

sources.title: Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998
sources.status: In force. Section 8(d) (certification of tests) was deleted with effect from 1 January 2025.

sources.title: Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008
sources.status: In force. Protects consumers in transactions within its scope, including against false, misleading or deceptive representations. Administered by the National Consumer Commission.

sources.title: Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020
sources.status: Most provisions commenced on 1 December 2021. Some sections, including section 54 (reporting by electronic communications service providers and financial institutions), were excluded from that commencement. NAVI could not confirm whether section 54 has since commenced: check before relying on it.

sources.title: King V Code on Corporate Governance for South Africa
sources.status: Released on 31 October 2025; applies to financial years starting on or after 1 January 2026 and replaces King IV. Voluntary and principle-based; organisations that claim to apply it must make disclosures under its Disclosure Framework. Listed companies should check how JSE Listings Requirements refer to it.

sources.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy (draft)
sources.status: Not in force. A draft published for comment in 2026 was withdrawn; a revised draft is expected to be published for public comment in January 2027. It is a policy document, not law.

sources.title: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR)
sources.status: Applies since 25 May 2018. Applies to organisations established in the EU and, under Article 3(2), to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Amendments proposed under the EU's 2025 Digital Omnibus package should be checked for current status.

sources.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
sources.status: In force since 1 August 2024 and applying in phases: prohibited practices and AI literacy from 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI obligations from 2 August 2025; Article 50 transparency from 2 August 2026; high-risk requirements for Annex III uses (e.g. employment, credit) from 2 December 2027 and for Annex I products from 2 August 2028, as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (dated 8 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026). Can apply to providers and deployers outside the EU where the AI system's output is used in the EU.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Artificial intelligence — Management system
sources.status: Published December 2023. Voluntary; organisations can choose to be certified.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 Artificial intelligence — Guidance on risk management
sources.status: Published 2023. Voluntary guidance; not certifiable.

sources.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.status: Released January 2023; version 1.0 remains the current framework, supplemented by profiles and guidance. Voluntary.

sources.title: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (OECD AI Principles)
sources.status: Adopted May 2019; updated May 2024. Non-binding intergovernmental standard.

sources.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
sources.status: Adopted November 2021 by UNESCO member states. Non-binding.

sources.title: NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework — Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
sources.publisher: US National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.status: Published July 2024. A companion profile to the NIST AI RMF for generative AI. Voluntary.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A: Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models
sources.publisher: US National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.status: Published July 2024 as a community profile of the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF, SP 800-218). Voluntary.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications (2025)
sources.status: 2025 edition, current. Community-maintained security guidance. Voluntary.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026
sources.status: Published 9 December 2025. Community-maintained security guidance for AI agents. Voluntary.

sources.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
sources.publisher: UK National Cyber Security Centre with international cyber agencies
sources.status: Version 1.0, published 27 November 2023. Voluntary.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems)
sources.status: Living knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI-enabled systems, based on real-world observations and demonstrations. Voluntary.

sources.title: Joint Standard 1 of 2023: IT Governance and Risk Management (FSCA and Prudential Authority)
sources.publisher: Financial Sector Conduct Authority and Prudential Authority (South Africa)
sources.scope: Financial institutions within the standard's scope (for example banks and insurers).
sources.status: Effective 15 November 2024. Binding on financial institutions within its scope.

sources.title: Joint Standard 2 of 2024: Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Requirements (FSCA and Prudential Authority)
sources.publisher: Financial Sector Conduct Authority and Prudential Authority (South Africa)
sources.scope: Financial institutions within the standard's scope, including banks, insurers and certain Category I FSPs, pension funds, section 13B administrators, OTC derivative providers and credit rating agencies.
sources.status: Commenced 1 June 2025, with 12 months to comply fully. Binding on financial institutions within its scope.

sources.title: Determination on reporting material IT and cyber incidents (FSCA and Prudential Authority)
sources.publisher: Financial Sector Conduct Authority and Prudential Authority (South Africa)
sources.scope: Financial institutions covered by Joint Standard 1 of 2023 or Joint Standard 2 of 2024.
sources.status: In effect from 1 September 2026, under the Financial Sector Regulation Act.

sources.title: Information Regulator remarks on AI and POPIA (September 2026)
sources.publisher: Information Regulator (South Africa), as reported by ITWeb
sources.status: Public remarks reported on 17 September 2026. Not guidance and not binding, but shows the regulator's concerns.

sources.title: Information Regulator: mandatory eServices Portal for security compromise notifications
sources.publisher: Information Regulator (South Africa), as reported by Covington
sources.scope: Responsible parties notifying a security compromise under POPIA section 22.
sources.status: Announced 7 April 2025: the eServices Portal is the official channel for security compromise notifications.

sources.title: PRA Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
sources.publisher: Bank of England Prudential Regulation Authority (UK)
sources.scope: Only UK banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval for regulatory capital. Useful good practice for everyone else.
sources.status: Current version took effect on 23 April 2026; the first version took effect on 17 May 2024. Explicitly covers AI and machine-learning models.

sources.title: New York City Local Law 144 of 2021: Automated Employment Decision Tools
sources.publisher: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
sources.scope: Employers and employment agencies using automated employment decision tools for candidates or employees in New York City.
sources.status: Enforced since 5 July 2023.

sources.title: NAVI good-practice notes
sources.status: NAVI's own practical guidance, drawing on the sources cited in each note. Good practice, not law.

passages.title: Conditions for lawful processing
passages.text: Personal information must be processed under eight conditions: accountability, processing limitation (including minimality and a lawful justification such as consent or legitimate interest), purpose specification, further-processing limitation, information quality, openness, security safeguards and data-subject participation.

passages.title: Automated decision making
passages.text: A person may not be subject to a decision that has legal consequences for them, or affects them to a substantial degree, if it is based solely on automated processing intended to profile them (e.g. performance at work, creditworthiness, reliability, location, health, personal preferences or conduct), unless an exception in s71(2) applies. Where the contract exception relies on appropriate measures, the person must be able to make representations and be given sufficient information about the underlying logic.
passages.uncertainty: Whether a decision is 'based solely' on automated processing depends on how meaningful the human involvement is. If the human role is limited or nominal, get legal advice.

passages.title: Security safeguards, operators and breach notification
passages.text: Take appropriate, reasonable technical and organisational measures to secure personal information (s19); ensure operators such as AI providers process it only with authorisation and under a written contract with security measures (ss20–21); notify the Information Regulator and affected people of security compromises (s22).

passages.title: Special personal information
passages.text: Processing special personal information (e.g. health, biometrics, race or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, trade union membership, political persuasion, sex life, criminal behaviour) is prohibited unless a general authorisation in s27 applies (e.g. explicit consent, or necessity for establishing a right or obligation in law).
passages.uncertainty: Which s27 authorisation applies depends on your context; confirm with your Information Officer or legal adviser.

passages.title: Personal information of children
passages.text: Processing children's personal information is prohibited unless a general authorisation in s35 applies, such as prior consent of a competent person (e.g. a parent or guardian).

passages.title: Transfers of personal information outside South Africa
passages.text: Personal information may not be transferred to a third party in a foreign country unless one of the s72(1) conditions is met: the recipient is bound by law, binding corporate rules or a binding agreement giving adequate protection; the person consents; the transfer is necessary for a contract; or it is for the person's benefit and consent is impracticable but likely.
passages.uncertainty: If the processing location is unknown, you cannot yet show that a s72 condition is met.

passages.title: Prior authorisation by the Information Regulator
passages.text: Certain processing needs the Information Regulator's prior authorisation, including transferring special personal information or children's personal information to a third party in a foreign country that does not provide an adequate level of protection.
passages.uncertainty: Applies only if the recipient country does not provide adequate protection. Confirm with your Information Officer or legal adviser.

passages.title: Direct marketing by electronic communication
passages.text: Direct marketing by unsolicited electronic communication (e.g. email or SMS) needs the person's consent, unless they are an existing customer who was given the chance to object.

passages.title: Access to records
passages.text: People may request access to records held by private bodies (subject to grounds for refusal), and private bodies must publish a PAIA manual. Records of AI-assisted decisions may be requested.
passages.uncertainty: Requirements differ for public and private bodies; confirm which applies.

passages.title: Prohibition of unfair discrimination
passages.text: No person may unfairly discriminate, directly or indirectly, against an employee in any employment policy or practice (section 9 extends this protection to applicants for employment) on listed grounds such as race, gender, sex, pregnancy, ethnic or social origin, colour, age, disability, religion, culture or language.

passages.title: Psychological testing and other similar assessments
passages.text: Psychological testing and other similar assessments of an employee are prohibited unless the test or assessment has been scientifically shown to be valid and reliable, can be applied fairly to all employees, and is not biased against any employee or group.
passages.uncertainty: Whether an AI screening or scoring tool is an 'other similar assessment' is not settled. Treat it as one unless advised otherwise.

passages.title: False, misleading or deceptive representations
passages.text: Suppliers must not make false, misleading or deceptive representations to consumers. AI-generated marketing or chatbot answers are the supplier's own representations.
passages.uncertainty: Applies to transactions within the Consumer Protection Act's scope; some transactions are excluded.

passages.title: Reporting of cybercrime by financial institutions and communications providers
passages.text: Requires electronic communications service providers and financial institutions to report, within 72 hours of becoming aware, offences under the Act involving their systems, and to preserve related information.
passages.uncertainty: Section 54 was not part of the 1 December 2021 commencement. NAVI could not confirm whether it has since commenced; check its status before relying on it.

passages.title: Board oversight of data, information, technology and AI
passages.text: King V expects the governing body to govern data, information and technology, including oversight of emerging technologies such as AI with attention to transparency, explainability and human-centred design, and risks from outsourced technology.
passages.uncertainty: Principle and practice numbering is based on secondary summaries; check the King V text for exact wording.

passages.title: National AI Policy (watch list)
passages.text: South Africa does not yet have a national AI policy in force. A revised draft is expected for public comment in January 2027. Monitor it; it creates no obligations today.

passages.title: Scope, principles and lawful basis
passages.text: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes, minimised, accurate, kept no longer than necessary and secured, with a lawful basis under Article 6.
passages.uncertainty: For organisations outside the EU, the GDPR applies only in the Article 3(2) situations. Confirm whether it applies to you.

passages.title: Special categories of personal data
passages.text: Processing special category data (e.g. health, biometric data used for identification, racial or ethnic origin) is prohibited unless an Article 9(2) condition applies.

passages.title: Automated individual decision-making
passages.text: People have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects, unless an exception applies with safeguards (at least human intervention, the ability to express a view and to contest).
passages.uncertainty: Applies only to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; meaningful human involvement takes a decision outside Article 22.

passages.title: Data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
passages.text: A DPIA is required before processing likely to result in a high risk to people, including systematic and extensive automated evaluation, large-scale special category data, and new technologies.

passages.title: Using a processor
passages.text: Processors such as AI providers must be engaged under a binding contract with the terms set out in Article 28.

passages.title: International transfers
passages.text: Transfers of personal data outside the EU/EEA need an adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards (e.g. standard contractual clauses) or a specific derogation.

passages.title: AI literacy
passages.text: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf. Applies since 2 February 2025.
passages.uncertainty: Whether the EU AI Act applies to a non-EU organisation depends on whether you place AI on the EU market or its output is used in the EU.

passages.title: Prohibited AI practices
passages.text: Certain practices are banned, including: manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm; exploiting vulnerabilities; social scoring; inferring emotions in the workplace or education (except for medical or safety reasons); untargeted scraping of facial images; biometric categorisation to infer sensitive traits; and, from 2 December 2026, AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material. Applies since 2 February 2025.
passages.uncertainty: Each prohibition has precise conditions and exceptions. Stop and get legal advice.

passages.section: Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 4; Article 26
passages.title: High-risk AI: employment and worker management
passages.text: AI used for recruitment or selection (e.g. filtering applications, evaluating candidates) or for decisions on promotion, termination, task allocation or monitoring and evaluating workers is high-risk. Deployers must use it according to instructions, assign competent human oversight, monitor it, keep logs and inform workers' representatives and affected workers. High-risk requirements for Annex III uses apply from 2 December 2027.
passages.uncertainty: Article 6(3) exempts some Annex III systems that do not pose a significant risk (e.g. narrow preparatory tasks). Obligations apply from 2 December 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

passages.title: High-risk AI: creditworthiness
passages.text: AI used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score (other than for detecting financial fraud) is high-risk. High-risk requirements for Annex III uses apply from 2 December 2027.
passages.uncertainty: Applies only if the AI evaluates creditworthiness or credit scores of individuals.

passages.title: Transparency for AI interactions and generated content
passages.text: People must be informed when they interact with an AI system (unless obvious); synthetic audio, image, video or text content must be marked as AI-generated by providers; deployers must disclose deep fakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. Applies from 2 August 2026.
passages.uncertainty: Generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 for machine-readable marking.

passages.title: AI management system
passages.text: A management-system approach: AI policy, roles and responsibilities, AI risk and impact assessment, lifecycle controls, monitoring and continual improvement.

passages.title: AI risk management
passages.text: Guidance for organisations that develop, produce, deploy or use AI on managing AI-specific risk and building risk management into their AI activities, across the lifecycle.

passages.title: AI risk management functions
passages.text: Govern (culture, roles, policies), Map (context and impacts), Measure (test and track risks, including bias) and Manage (prioritise and act on risks).

passages.title: Trustworthy AI principles
passages.text: Inclusive growth and well-being; human rights and democratic values including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability.

passages.title: Ethics of AI, including environmental sustainability
passages.text: Human rights and dignity, fairness and non-discrimination, human oversight, transparency, privacy, and environmental and ecosystem flourishing across the AI lifecycle.

passages.title: Purpose and lawful basis documented
passages.text: The reason for using the AI and the legal justification for any personal information are written down. What to do: Document the purpose of the AI use case and the lawful justification for processing personal information. Suggested owner: Business owner with the Information Officer / DPO.

passages.title: Only necessary data is used
passages.text: Inputs are limited to what the use case needs; personal details are removed or masked where possible. What to do: Limit inputs to the minimum information needed; remove or mask personal details where possible. Suggested owner: Business owner.

passages.title: Affected people are told
passages.text: Customers, staff or applicants are informed that AI is used and how. What to do: Tell affected people that AI is used, for what, and how to raise concerns (update privacy notices). Suggested owner: Information Officer / DPO.

passages.title: Impact assessment completed
passages.text: A data protection / AI impact assessment has been done and signed off. What to do: Complete and sign off a data protection or AI impact assessment before go-live. Suggested owner: Information Officer / DPO.

passages.title: Meaningful human review
passages.text: A competent person reviews AI outputs and can override them before they affect anyone. What to do: Put a competent person in the loop who reviews and can override AI outputs before they take effect. Suggested owner: Business owner.

passages.title: People can query or contest outcomes
passages.text: Affected people can ask for an explanation and challenge a decision. What to do: Give affected people a route to request an explanation and to contest AI-influenced decisions. Suggested owner: Business owner.

passages.title: Contract with the AI provider
passages.text: A contract or data processing agreement covers security, confidentiality and no training on your data. What to do: Put a written contract / data processing agreement in place with the AI provider covering security, confidentiality, sub-processors and no training on your data. Suggested owner: Procurement with Legal.

passages.title: Cross-border transfer safeguard
passages.text: A lawful basis exists for sending data to another country (adequate protection, binding agreement, consent, etc.). What to do: Confirm a lawful basis for sending personal information across borders (e.g. adequate protection or a binding agreement) before transfer. Suggested owner: Information Officer / DPO with Legal.

passages.title: Security controls and logging
passages.text: Access control, logging and a security review of the AI tool are in place. What to do: Apply access controls and logging, and complete a security review of the AI tool and its integrations. Suggested owner: CISO / IT security.

passages.title: Incident response covers AI
passages.text: Incident and breach procedures include AI failures and data leaks. What to do: Extend incident and breach-response procedures to cover AI failures, misuse and data leaks. Suggested owner: CISO / IT security.

passages.title: Bias and accuracy testing
passages.text: Outputs have been tested for accuracy and for unfair differences between groups. What to do: Test outputs for accuracy and for unfair differences between groups before go-live and after changes. Suggested owner: Data / AI team.

passages.title: Users are trained
passages.text: People using the AI understand its limits and their responsibilities. What to do: Train users on the tool's limits, verification of outputs and their responsibilities. Suggested owner: Business owner with HR / Learning.

passages.title: Recorded in an AI register with an owner
passages.text: The use case is logged with a named accountable owner. What to do: Record the use case in an AI register with a named accountable owner and review date. Suggested owner: AI governance lead.

passages.title: Ongoing monitoring
passages.text: Accuracy, complaints and drift are monitored after go-live. What to do: Monitor accuracy, complaints and drift after go-live, with a scheduled review. Suggested owner: Business owner.

passages.title: AI interaction and content are disclosed
passages.text: People know when they are dealing with AI or AI-generated content. What to do: Disclose to people when they are interacting with AI or viewing AI-generated content. Suggested owner: Business owner.

passages.title: Safeguards for children's information
passages.text: Parental consent or another lawful basis and extra protections are in place for children. What to do: Obtain a lawful basis such as competent-person (parental) consent and apply extra protections for children's information. Suggested owner: Information Officer / DPO.

passages.title: Characteristics of trustworthy AI
passages.text: The NIST AI RMF describes trustworthy AI as valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; and fair, with harmful bias managed. Validity and reliability are the base for the others, and accountability and transparency apply across all of them. Trade-offs between them, such as accuracy against interpretability, should be decided deliberately and documented.

passages.title: Govern: policies, accountability and culture
passages.text: GOVERN is the cross-cutting function: policies and processes for AI risk are in place and followed; accountability structures make sure the right people are empowered, responsible and trained; workforce diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility are prioritised in AI risk decisions; the culture supports raising and acting on risks; the organisation engages with relevant AI actors and outside feedback; and risks and benefits from third-party software, data and supply chains are addressed, including contingency plans.

passages.title: Map: understanding context and impacts
passages.text: MAP establishes the context before risks are measured: the intended purpose and setting, who uses and is affected by the system, its capabilities and limits, the benefits and costs, and the likely impacts on individuals, groups, organisations and society. Mapping well is what makes it possible to decide whether a system should be built or deployed at all.

passages.title: Measure: testing, evaluation, verification and validation
passages.text: MEASURE uses quantitative and qualitative methods to analyse and track AI risks: choosing appropriate metrics, testing before deployment and regularly in operation, evaluating the trustworthy characteristics (including bias, robustness, security and privacy), involving independent assessors where appropriate, and tracking risks that are hard to measure.

passages.title: Manage: acting on risks, including after deployment
passages.text: MANAGE allocates resources to the risks mapped and measured: deciding whether to proceed, treating prioritised risks, planning responses to and recovery from incidents, managing risks from third-party components, and monitoring systems after deployment, including mechanisms to capture user feedback, handle appeals, and decommission or override systems that perform badly.

passages.title: Twelve risks specific to or worsened by generative AI
passages.text: The NIST Generative AI Profile lists twelve risks: CBRN information or capabilities; confabulation (confident false output); dangerous, violent or hateful content; data privacy; environmental impacts; harmful bias and homogenisation; human-AI configuration (such as over-reliance and anthropomorphising); information integrity; information security; intellectual property; obscene, degrading or abusive content; and value chain and component integration (risks from third-party models and data).

passages.title: Four priority areas for generative AI governance
passages.text: The profile highlights four areas: governance (policies and oversight that cover generative AI, including third-party tools), content provenance (tracking where content came from and whether it was AI-generated), pre-deployment testing (including red-teaming and evaluation in realistic conditions), and incident disclosure (recording and sharing information about AI incidents).

passages.title: Leadership and AI policy
passages.text: ISO/IEC 42001 expects top management to demonstrate leadership of the AI management system, set an AI policy that fits the organisation's purpose and includes commitments to meet requirements and improve, and assign roles, responsibilities and authorities. Certification is voluntary; the clauses are also a useful checklist for organisations that do not seek certification.

passages.title: AI risk and impact assessment and lifecycle controls
passages.text: The standard requires an AI risk assessment, risk treatment and an AI system impact assessment that considers consequences for individuals, groups and society. Its Annex A reference controls cover areas such as AI policies, internal organisation, resources for AI systems, impact assessment, the AI system lifecycle, data for AI systems, information for interested parties, responsible use, and third-party and customer relationships.

passages.title: Board oversight of AI under King V
passages.text: King V expects the governing body to govern technology and information, including emerging technologies such as AI, so that they support the organisation's objectives ethically and within its risk appetite. In practice boards should know where AI is used, approve the organisation's stance on AI, receive regular reporting on material AI risks and incidents, and make sure accountability for each significant AI system sits with management.
passages.uncertainty: Based on secondary summaries of King V; check the King V text for exact principles and practices.

passages.title: Questions a board should ask about AI
passages.text: Useful board questions: Where are we using AI today, including staff use of public tools? Which uses are high-impact for customers, employees or our licence to operate? Who is accountable for each? What is our risk appetite for AI, and what will we not do? Which laws apply (for example POPIA, and the EU AI Act if we serve the EU)? How are AI suppliers vetted? How do we know the systems are working as intended, and what are our AI incidents? Do directors and staff have enough AI literacy? These align with King V's technology governance principles, NIST AI RMF GOVERN and ISO/IEC 42001 leadership clauses.

passages.title: Starting an AI strategy that governance can support
passages.text: A practical AI strategy names the business problems AI should help with; sets a risk appetite (uses the organisation will pursue, approach with conditions, or avoid); funds data quality, skills and security as prerequisites; defines how new AI uses are proposed, assessed and approved; and sets measures of value and harm. Governance should be proportionate: light-touch for low-risk productivity uses and thorough for uses that affect people's rights, money or safety.

passages.title: Keep an AI inventory
passages.text: An AI inventory (or register) lists every AI system and significant AI use: its purpose, owner, supplier or model, data used, people affected, risk rating, safeguards, approval date and next review. It is the foundation for oversight, incident response, regulatory questions and audits. The EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001 and model risk guidance such as PRA SS1/23 all assume one exists.

passages.title: Due diligence questions for AI suppliers
passages.text: Before using a third-party AI service, ask: Is our data used to train or improve their models, and can that be switched off? Where is data processed and stored, and for how long? Who are their subprocessors? What security certifications and testing do they have? How do they handle incidents and tell us? What documentation do they give about the model's capabilities, limits and testing? Can we get logs? What happens to our data when the contract ends? Record the answers and reflect them in the contract (POPIA sections 20 and 21; GDPR Article 28; EU AI Act Article 25(4) for high-risk components).

passages.title: Contract terms for AI services
passages.text: Contracts for AI services that touch personal or confidential information should cover: processing only on your instructions; no training on your data without agreement; security measures; breach notification to you without delay; subprocessor approval; location of processing and transfer safeguards; audit or assurance rights; support for data-subject requests; return or deletion at the end; and, where relevant, documentation needed for your own regulatory obligations.

passages.title: Data governance for AI
passages.text: Good AI data governance means knowing what data feeds each system and where it came from; checking that you are allowed to use it for this purpose (POPIA purpose specification and further-processing limits; GDPR purpose limitation); using only the data needed; checking quality and representativeness for the people affected; protecting it in training, retrieval and logs; setting retention periods; and recording all of this so it can be explained later. The EU AI Act's Article 10 sets these expectations formally for high-risk systems.

passages.title: Retention of prompts, outputs and logs
passages.text: AI systems create new records: prompts, outputs, retrieved documents and logs. Decide how long each is kept and why, balancing record-keeping needs (such as the EU AI Act's minimum six months for deployer logs of high-risk systems) against privacy law's limits on keeping personal information longer than necessary (POPIA section 14; GDPR Article 5(1)(e)). Check the supplier's retention too.

passages.title: Testing an AI system before release
passages.text: Before release, test against what matters for the use: accuracy on realistic cases, including edge cases; performance across relevant groups of people (bias testing); robustness to unusual or adversarial input, including prompt injection for language models; refusal and safe behaviour on out-of-scope requests; privacy leakage; and, for generative AI, factual accuracy against trusted sources. Write acceptance criteria before testing, keep a held-out test set that is not used for tuning, and record results and who approved release. Sources: NIST AI RMF MEASURE, NIST AI 600-1 and the OWASP LLM Top 10.

passages.title: Red-teaming AI systems
passages.text: Red-teaming means deliberately trying to make the system fail or misbehave: extracting confidential data, bypassing instructions, producing harmful or false content, or misusing an agent's tools. Use people who understand both the domain and attack techniques, use MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP lists as checklists, record every finding, fix or accept each with a named owner, and repeat after significant changes.

passages.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity of high-risk AI
passages.text: High-risk AI systems must achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout their lifecycle, with accuracy levels declared in the instructions for use. They should be resilient to errors and to attempts to alter their use or performance, such as data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks. Systems that keep learning after deployment must manage the risk of biased feedback loops.
passages.uncertainty: Applies to high-risk AI systems; Annex III high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027.

passages.title: Deploying AI responsibly
passages.text: Roll out in stages: a limited pilot with close review, then wider use once agreed measures are met. Before go-live, confirm approval and ownership, train users on limits and when to override, tell affected people where required, set up monitoring and a way to report problems, document a rollback plan, and treat model or prompt changes as changes that need testing and approval.

passages.title: Monitoring AI after deployment
passages.text: Monitor what you tested: accuracy or error rates on sampled cases, outcomes across groups of people, drift in input data or behaviour, complaints and override rates, security events, cost and usage, and supplier changes to the model. Set thresholds that trigger review, report regularly to the accountable owner, and re-assess the system at least annually or after significant change. NIST AI RMF MANAGE and the EU AI Act's deployer monitoring duty (Article 26) set similar expectations.

passages.title: Post-market monitoring by providers
passages.text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must have a post-market monitoring system that actively and systematically collects and analyses data on how the system performs throughout its life, so they can check continued compliance, based on a documented post-market monitoring plan.
passages.uncertainty: Paragraph 3 (the monitoring plan and the Commission's template, due by 2 September 2027) was amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

passages.title: Handling AI incidents
passages.text: An AI incident is any event where an AI system caused or nearly caused harm, such as a wrong decision about a person, a data leak, harmful output, or an agent acting outside its limits. Prepare in advance: define what counts as an incident, who decides severity, how to pause the system, and which reporting duties may apply (for example POPIA section 22, the South African financial-sector 24-hour reporting, GDPR Article 33, or EU AI Act Article 73). Afterwards, record the cause and the fixes, and update the risk assessment.

passages.title: Independent validation of AI models
passages.text: Model validation is an independent check that a model is conceptually sound, performs as intended on relevant data, is used within its limits, and is monitored. For AI, validators should also look at data quality and representativeness, explainability, stability over time, sensitivity to small input changes and fairness. The depth of validation should follow the model's risk tier. PRA SS1/23 Principle 4 sets out this expectation for banks.

passages.title: Explaining AI-assisted decisions
passages.text: People affected by AI-assisted decisions should be able to understand, at a suitable level, that AI was involved, what it considered, how it affected the outcome, and how to ask for human review. Explanations should be prepared for each audience: the person affected, the staff member relying on the output, and auditors or regulators. POPIA section 71(3), GDPR Articles 13 to 15 and 22, and EU AI Act Articles 26(11) and 86 all point in this direction.

passages.title: Managing bias and unfair discrimination
passages.text: Bias can come from historical data, from which groups are under-represented, from proxies for protected characteristics (such as postal code), or from how outputs are used. Identify the groups that matter in context (in South Africa including those protected under the Employment Equity Act), test outcomes across them before and after deployment, investigate differences, keep a person able to override, and document the decisions made.

passages.title: AI literacy for staff
passages.text: Staff who use or oversee AI need to know what it can and cannot do, common failure modes such as confident errors and bias, the organisation's rules for AI use, how to protect personal and confidential information, and when to override or escalate. Training should match the role: basic awareness for everyone, deeper training for people who approve, oversee or build AI. The EU AI Act's Article 4 makes AI literacy measures a legal duty for providers and deployers in its scope.

passages.title: Data and data governance for high-risk AI
passages.text: Providers of high-risk AI systems that train models must apply data governance practices to training, validation and testing data. These cover design choices, data collection and origin, preparation such as labelling and cleaning, assumptions, and data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and, as far as possible, error-free and complete for the intended purpose, and must reflect the setting where the system will be used. Providers must examine data for biases that could harm health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, and take measures to detect, prevent and reduce them. Where a system does not involve model training, these requirements apply to testing data. A new Article 4a deals with processing special categories of personal data for bias detection.
passages.uncertainty: High-risk requirements for Annex III uses apply from 2 December 2027. Check Article 4a for the conditions on using special category data.

passages.title: Human oversight of high-risk AI
passages.text: High-risk AI systems must be designed so people can oversee them effectively while in use, in proportion to the risk, autonomy and context. The people overseeing must be able to understand the system's capabilities and limits and spot anomalies; stay aware of automation bias (over-relying on the output); interpret the output correctly; decide not to use it or override it; and intervene or stop the system safely. For remote biometric identification, no action may be taken unless at least two competent people separately verify the identification, with limited exceptions.
passages.uncertainty: Applies to high-risk AI systems; Annex III high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027.

passages.title: When a deployer becomes a provider; value-chain agreements
passages.text: A deployer, distributor, importer or other party takes on the full provider obligations if it puts its own name or trademark on a high-risk AI system, substantially modifies one, or changes the intended purpose of an AI system (including a general-purpose one) so that it becomes high-risk. The original provider must then cooperate, for example by sharing documentation and known limitations. Providers of high-risk systems and their suppliers of AI components must agree in writing on the information, access and help needed for compliance.
passages.uncertainty: Paragraphs 1 to 4 were amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; check the consolidated text for exact wording.

passages.title: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI
passages.text: Organisations using (deploying) high-risk AI must: use it according to the provider's instructions; assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training, authority and support; make sure input data they control is relevant and sufficiently representative; monitor the system and tell the provider and authorities about risks or serious incidents, suspending use where it may present a risk; keep the logs they control for at least six months; inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using it at work; inform people when a high-risk Annex III system makes or helps make decisions about them; use the provider's information for any GDPR data protection impact assessment; and cooperate with authorities.
passages.uncertainty: Annex III high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027. Financial institutions can meet some duties through their financial-sector governance rules.

passages.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
passages.text: Before first using certain high-risk AI systems, public bodies, private bodies providing public services, and deployers of AI for creditworthiness or life and health insurance pricing must assess the impact on fundamental rights. The assessment describes how and how often the system will be used, who is likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm, how human oversight will work, and what will be done if risks materialise, including complaint mechanisms. Results are notified to the market surveillance authority. An existing GDPR data protection impact assessment can be cross-referenced.
passages.uncertainty: Paragraphs 4 and 5 were amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Applies from the Annex III high-risk date (2 December 2027).

passages.title: Obligations of general-purpose AI model providers
passages.text: Providers of general-purpose AI models (such as large language models) must keep technical documentation, give downstream developers the information they need to understand the model's capabilities and limits, have a policy to comply with EU copyright law including rights reservations, and publish a summary of training content using the AI Office template. Open-source models are exempt from the documentation duties unless they pose systemic risk. These obligations apply from 2 August 2025. Organisations that only use such models through a product are not GPAI providers, but can ask their supplier for this information.
passages.uncertainty: Models with systemic risk have extra duties under Article 55.

passages.title: Reporting serious incidents
passages.text: Providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority of the member state where they occurred: immediately once a causal link is established or reasonably likely, and no later than 15 days after becoming aware. The limit is 2 days for widespread infringements or serious disruption of critical infrastructure, and 10 days where a person has died. An incomplete first report can be followed by a complete one. Deployers who find a serious incident must inform the provider first.

passages.title: Penalties
passages.text: Maximum fines are EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; EUR 15 million or 3% for breaching most other obligations, including deployer duties and Article 50 transparency; and EUR 7.5 million or 1% for giving incorrect or misleading information to authorities. The higher amount applies, except for SMEs and start-ups, where the lower applies.

passages.title: When the EU AI Act reaches organisations outside the EU
passages.text: The Act applies to providers placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market, wherever they are established, and to providers and deployers outside the EU where the output produced by the AI system is used in the EU. A South African organisation using AI only for South African customers is generally outside scope; one offering AI-enabled services to people in the EU, or whose AI outputs are used there, should check.
passages.uncertainty: Scope questions turn on facts; get legal advice for cross-border services.

passages.title: Explaining automated decisions to people
passages.text: Where Article 22 automated decision-making, including profiling, takes place, people must be told it exists and be given meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences for them, both when data is collected and when they ask for access to their data.

passages.title: Data protection by design and by default
passages.text: Controllers must build data protection into the design of processing, for example through pseudonymisation and data minimisation, and by default process only the personal data necessary for each purpose. For AI this means deciding early what data the system truly needs, how long it is kept and who can see it.

passages.title: Security and personal data breaches
passages.text: Controllers and processors must secure personal data with measures appropriate to the risk. A personal data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. Where the risk to people is high, they must also be told without undue delay.

passages.title: When POPIA applies
passages.text: POPIA applies to processing personal information entered in a record by a responsible party domiciled in South Africa, or by one not domiciled here that uses automated or non-automated means in South Africa (unless only to forward information through the country). Using an overseas AI service does not take processing outside POPIA; the South African organisation remains the responsible party.

passages.title: Telling people about processing
passages.text: When collecting personal information, a responsible party must take reasonable steps to make the person aware of matters such as what is collected, the purpose, whether supply is voluntary or mandatory, any law requiring it, any intended cross-border transfer, and their rights. If AI processing is a new purpose or involves sending data abroad, privacy notices may need updating.

passages.title: Notifying security compromises
passages.text: Where there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person, the responsible party must notify the Information Regulator and the affected people as soon as reasonably possible. The notice to people should describe the possible consequences, the measures taken, what they can do to reduce harm, and, if known, who accessed the information. Operators (such as AI providers) must tell the responsible party immediately.

passages.title: Reporting breaches through the Regulator's eServices Portal
passages.text: Since April 2025 the Information Regulator has required security compromise notifications to be submitted through its eServices Portal. Information Officers should register for the portal before an incident happens so that reporting is not delayed.

passages.title: Exceptions and safeguards for automated decisions
passages.text: The section 71 prohibition does not apply where the decision is taken in connection with a contract and the person's request was met, or appropriate measures protect their legitimate interests; or where a law or code of conduct authorises it with such measures. Appropriate measures must give the person an opportunity to make representations about the decision and give them sufficient information about the underlying logic of the automated processing.

passages.title: The Information Officer's role
passages.text: Every responsible party has an Information Officer (by default the head of the organisation) who must encourage and ensure compliance with POPIA, deal with requests and work with the Regulator, and who must be registered with the Regulator. Deputy Information Officers can be designated. New AI uses of personal information should be brought to the Information Officer before they start.

passages.title: Administrative fines
passages.text: The Information Regulator may impose administrative fines of up to R10 million for certain offences under POPIA. Some offences also carry possible imprisonment. Regulators can also issue enforcement notices requiring processing to stop or change.

passages.title: What the Information Regulator has said about AI
passages.text: In September 2026 the Information Regulator's leadership highlighted consent, retention and transparency as key AI challenges, said AI models often keep personal information beyond its intended purpose, questioned whether privacy-by-default and personal information impact assessments actually happen, and called for audits of how AI systems process personal information in South Africa. It also said POPIA does not stand in the way of innovation. These are remarks, not guidance, but signal what the Regulator is likely to look for.

passages.title: IT governance and risk management for financial institutions
passages.text: Joint Standard 1 of 2023 requires financial institutions within scope to govern and manage IT risk, covering IT strategy, risk management, IT operations, resilience, business continuity and assurance. AI systems are IT systems, so a bank or insurer deploying AI should bring it within these governance, change-management and resilience processes.
passages.uncertainty: Summary based on a secondary source. Check the standard's text for exact requirements and scope.

passages.title: Cybersecurity and cyber resilience for financial institutions
passages.text: Joint Standard 2 of 2024 requires financial institutions within scope to maintain a regularly reviewed cybersecurity strategy; identify critical processes and information assets; control access, including multi-factor authentication for critical system functions; prevent data loss; patch and protect endpoints; back up data securely; monitor, detect, respond to and recover from attacks; regularly test their controls; and notify the regulator of material cyber incidents. AI services and the data they use fall within these requirements.
passages.uncertainty: Summary based on secondary sources. Check the standard's text for exact requirements and scope.

passages.title: Reporting material IT and cyber incidents within 24 hours
passages.text: From 1 September 2026, financial institutions covered by Joint Standards 1 of 2023 or 2 of 2024 must notify the Prudential Authority or FSCA within 24 hours (weekends and public holidays included) after classifying an IT or cyber incident as material, update within 14 calendar days, and submit a final report within an agreed period. Outsourcing, including to an AI provider, does not transfer this responsibility. POPIA breach notification still applies separately.
passages.uncertainty: Summary based on a secondary source. Institutions decide materiality using their own documented criteria.

passages.title: Bias audits for automated hiring tools in New York City
passages.text: Employers and employment agencies using an automated employment decision tool for candidates or employees in New York City must have had the tool bias-audited within the past year, publish a summary of the audit results, and give candidates or employees notice, at least 10 business days before use according to the city's guidance. Enforced since 5 July 2023. It is an example of the growing number of local rules on AI in hiring.

passages.title: Model risk management principles
passages.text: SS1/23 sets five principles: (1) identify models and classify their risk, keeping a model inventory; (2) governance, with board-level accountability and a senior manager responsible for model risk; (3) sound model development, implementation and use, including documentation and testing; (4) independent model validation before use and periodically after; and (5) model risk mitigants, such as limits on use, adjustments and heightened monitoring where weaknesses are known. It explicitly covers AI and machine-learning models. Although binding only on certain UK banks, it is a widely used benchmark for model risk management elsewhere.

passages.title: Working out which laws apply across countries
passages.text: For an AI use that crosses borders, check each of these separately: where your organisation is established (for example POPIA for South African responsible parties); where the affected people are (the GDPR can apply under Article 3(2) to offering services to, or monitoring, people in the EU); where the AI's output is used (the EU AI Act can apply when output is used in the EU); where data is processed or stored (POPIA section 72 and GDPR Chapter V transfer rules); and any sector rules (such as South Africa's financial-sector Joint Standards or New York City's hiring-tool law). Apply the strictest overlapping requirement where you can, and record which regimes you assessed.

passages.title: Prompt injection
passages.text: Prompt injection happens when text given to a language model, directly by a user or indirectly through a web page, document or email the model reads, changes its behaviour against the developer's intent. It can leak data, bypass safeguards or trigger actions. Mitigations include constraining the model's role in the system prompt, treating all external content as untrusted, separating and labelling untrusted input, filtering inputs and outputs, giving the model the least privilege it needs, requiring human approval for high-risk actions, and adversarial testing.

passages.title: Sensitive information disclosure
passages.text: Language model applications can reveal personal information, confidential business data or credentials through their outputs, for example from training data, retrieved documents or earlier conversation context. Mitigations include keeping sensitive data out of prompts and training data where possible, redacting or tokenising it, strict access control on retrieved content, clear user terms on how inputs are used, and output filtering.

passages.title: Supply chain
passages.text: Third-party models, datasets, fine-tuning adapters, plug-ins and libraries can be tampered with, outdated or carry unclear licences. Mitigations include vetting suppliers and their terms, keeping an inventory of components (a software or AI bill of materials), using models only from verifiable sources, checking integrity, and testing third-party models before use.

passages.title: Data and model poisoning
passages.text: Attackers can manipulate pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data to plant backdoors, biases or vulnerabilities. Mitigations include tracking data origin and transformations, validating and sandboxing data sources, monitoring training for anomalies, and red-team testing for hidden triggers before release.

passages.title: Improper output handling
passages.text: Passing model output to other systems without validation can cause cross-site scripting, SQL injection, remote code execution or privilege escalation. Treat model output like untrusted user input: validate and encode it for its destination, use parameterised queries, and apply content security policies.

passages.title: Excessive agency
passages.text: An AI agent or plug-in given too much functionality, too many permissions or too much autonomy can take damaging actions when it is manipulated or simply wrong. Limit the tools and functions available, give each tool the narrowest permissions, act with the user's own authorisation rather than a broad service account, require human approval for consequential actions, and log and monitor what the agent does.

passages.title: System prompt leakage
passages.text: System prompts can be extracted, so they must not contain secrets such as credentials or connection strings, or be relied on as a security control. Enforce access control and business rules outside the model.

passages.title: Vector and embedding weaknesses
passages.text: Retrieval-augmented generation systems can leak data across users or tenants, be poisoned through the documents they index, or have embeddings inverted to recover source text. Use permission-aware retrieval, partition data by user or tenant, validate documents before indexing, and log retrieval activity.

passages.title: Misinformation
passages.text: Models can produce false or fabricated content that sounds credible (often called hallucination), and users may over-rely on it. Mitigations include grounding answers in trusted sources, cross-checking critical outputs, human review where errors matter, telling users about limitations, and designing interfaces that encourage verification.

passages.title: Unbounded consumption
passages.text: Uncontrolled use of a model application can cause denial of service, runaway cost (sometimes called denial of wallet) or model extraction through mass querying. Mitigations include input size limits, rate limiting and quotas, timeouts, budget caps, and monitoring usage for anomalies.

passages.title: Agent goal hijack
passages.text: An attacker redirects an agent's objective through content the agent reads, such as an email, web page or document containing hidden instructions. Treat everything the agent reads as untrusted, keep goals and permissions fixed outside the model, and require confirmation before actions that depart from the user's request.

passages.title: Tool misuse and exploitation
passages.text: Legitimate tools an agent is allowed to use can be steered toward harmful outcomes, for example deleting records or sending data externally. Allow only the tools a task needs, validate tool parameters, set limits on scope and volume, and require human approval for irreversible or high-impact tool calls.

passages.title: Identity and privilege abuse
passages.text: If an agent holds broad credentials or inherits a user's full access, anyone who manipulates it inherits that access too. Give each agent its own identity, use short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, and separate what the agent can read from what it can change.

passages.title: Agentic supply chain vulnerabilities
passages.text: Agent frameworks, tool servers (such as MCP servers), plug-ins and other agents introduce risk, and the chain can change while the agent runs. Keep an inventory of components, pin and verify versions, vet third-party tool servers, and restrict which ones an agent may connect to.

passages.title: Unexpected code execution
passages.text: Agents that write or run code can turn natural-language input into executable code outside intended boundaries. Run generated code only in isolated sandboxes with no access to production credentials or networks unless explicitly needed, and review code before it reaches production.

passages.title: Memory and context poisoning
passages.text: False or malicious information planted in an agent's memory or context can influence later decisions, possibly for other users. Validate what is written to memory, separate memory by user, expire it, and keep an audit trail of memory changes.

passages.title: Insecure inter-agent communication
passages.text: When agents exchange messages without authentication or integrity checks, messages can be spoofed or altered. Authenticate agents, sign or otherwise protect messages, and validate what one agent accepts from another.

passages.title: Cascading failures
passages.text: One error or compromise can spread through connected agents and automated workflows faster than people notice. Add checkpoints between steps, limit how many actions can run without review, set circuit breakers, and monitor for unusual chains of activity.

passages.title: Human-agent trust exploitation
passages.text: Agent outputs can persuade people to approve unsafe actions, especially when approval requests are frequent or poorly explained. Show clearly what an approval will do, keep approvals meaningful rather than routine, and train reviewers to question agent recommendations.

passages.title: Rogue agents
passages.text: Agents can act outside policy while appearing legitimate, through compromise or misalignment. Keep a register of deployed agents and their owners, monitor behaviour against expected patterns, and make sure every agent can be paused or shut down quickly.

passages.title: Secure design of AI systems
passages.text: The guidelines start with design: raise staff awareness of AI-specific threats, model the threats to your system, and weigh security against functionality and performance when choosing an architecture and model. Decisions such as whether to use a hosted model or an open model, and what the AI may do, should be made with security in mind from the start.

passages.title: Secure development of AI systems
passages.text: Secure the supply chain for models, data and libraries; identify, track and protect AI assets such as models, weights, datasets and prompts; document how models and data were created, including known limitations; and manage technical debt.

passages.title: Secure deployment of AI systems
passages.text: Protect infrastructure and models from compromise, threat or loss; prepare incident management procedures; and release models and systems responsibly, only after appropriate security evaluation such as red-teaming. Make the secure configuration the default for users.

passages.title: Secure operation and maintenance
passages.text: Once live, log and monitor the system's inputs, outputs and behaviour to spot attacks and drift, manage updates securely (treating model updates like other changes, with testing), and share information about vulnerabilities and lessons learned.

passages.title: Secure development practices for generative AI
passages.text: SP 800-218A (July 2024) adds AI-specific practices to NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, which is organised into four groups: prepare the organisation, protect software, produce well-secured software, and respond to vulnerabilities. The AI additions include protecting training, testing, fine-tuning and alignment data and model weights from unauthorised access and change; tracking the provenance of data and models; analysing data for poisoning, bias and tampering; testing models for vulnerabilities through red-teaming and adversarial testing; and handling model vulnerabilities through vulnerability response, including criteria for when to stop using a model or roll back.

passages.title: Protecting model weights and training data
passages.text: Model weights, training data and configuration are valuable assets and attack targets. Store them with access control and integrity protection, record where they came from and how they were changed, and include them in backup and incident-response plans.

passages.title: Threat modelling AI systems with MITRE ATLAS
passages.text: MITRE ATLAS is a publicly accessible, continuously updated knowledge base of tactics and techniques that adversaries use against AI-enabled systems, based on real-world attack observations and demonstrations by AI red teams and security groups. It is modelled on, and complements, MITRE ATT&CK. Teams use it for threat modelling, red-team planning, choosing mitigations and reporting real-world attacks, and it includes case studies.

passages.title: Minimum controls before letting an AI agent act
passages.text: Before an AI agent can act on its own: (1) name an accountable owner and record the agent in your AI inventory; (2) list the tools and data it may use and deny everything else; (3) give it its own narrowly scoped, short-lived credentials; (4) require human approval for actions that are irreversible, financial, customer-facing or affect someone's rights; (5) set limits on volume, spend and run time; (6) log every action with enough detail to reconstruct what happened; (7) provide a tested way to pause or stop it; (8) test it against prompt injection and tool misuse before release. These reflect OWASP's agentic guidance and LLM06 (excessive agency).

passages.title: Acceptable use of public generative AI tools
passages.text: Staff often use free or personal versions of public AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude for work. A short acceptable-use rule prevents most early problems: say which tools are approved; forbid entering personal information, client data, credentials or confidential material into tools without an organisational agreement; require people to check outputs before relying on them; say when AI use must be disclosed; and name who to ask. Business or enterprise editions with contractual data protections are usually needed for any confidential or personal information.

passages.title: Developer checklist for building with language models
passages.text: For developers building on language models: keep API keys on a server, never in client code or repositories; treat all model input and output as untrusted; keep secrets out of prompts; enforce permissions outside the model; log prompts and outputs with care for personal data; set token, rate and cost limits; pin model versions and re-test when they change; build an evaluation set and run it on every change; and red-team for prompt injection, data leakage and harmful output before release. Sources: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), NIST SP 800-218A and the NCSC secure AI development guidelines.
